name: counting-semaphore
intent: Cap the concurrent use of a finite resource by handing out a fixed number of permits: every operation performs the equivalent of Dijkstra's P/acquire before touching the resource and the equivalent of V/release on every exit path, so at most N operations are inside at once instead of concurrency growing without limit.
problem: A finite resource - a connection pool, file handles, memory, a downstream API - degrades or fails when too many operations use it at once, but the call sites have no shared, enforceable notion of 'too many': thread-per-request designs, fan-out loops and retry bursts each add concurrency independently, so the resource is oversubscribed exactly when it is least able to cope. A per-second rate limit does not fix this, because ten slow operations saturate such a resource just as thoroughly as a thousand fast ones; what is needed is a bound on simultaneous use, expressed as one number the code enforces at a single admission point.
context: Concurrent, thread- or task-based software in which one shared resource has a hard or empirical concurrency ceiling: service clients with connection pools, workers that open files or sockets, caches with bounded builders, batch fan-out against an API with a quota. The decision is local to the code that uses the resource - a permit counter plus a release discipline, not distributed coordination - and it complements rather than replaces rate limiting, timeouts and circuit breakers.
benefits: Caps real resource consumption, not arrival rate: however fast operations arrive, at most N hold the resource, which is what connection pools, file descriptors, memory budgets and downstream quotas actually limit.
Turns overload into bounded queueing (or an explicit fast rejection) instead of cascading failure: excess operations wait for a permit instead of piling onto a saturated resource.
One admission point for heterogeneous callers: every path that touches the resource acquires from the same counter, so the bound cannot be evaded by adding a new call site.
Separates the admission policy from the resource owner: the pool or client stays simple, while the concurrency budget becomes a configurable, measurable number.
Weighted permits let one counter cover variable-size work - a request that needs k units acquires k - which a mutex or a fixed worker pool cannot express.
A one-permit semaphore is an ownership-free mutex: the permit may be released by a different thread or context, which is what hand-off and deadlock-recovery scenarios need.

Supports context cancellation natively in many implementations (Java Semaphore.tryAcquire, Go golang.org/x/sync/semaphore.Weighted.Acquire with context), preventing leaked permits when callers are cancelled.
Enables natural backpressure: producers that cannot acquire a permit slow down without buffering unboundedly, unlike a plain queue which can grow until memory is exhausted.
tradeoffs: Permits are anonymous: the semaphore counts holders, it does not know which item of a pool each holder owns, so handing out a specific free item still needs separate bookkeeping.

Release is not ownership-checked and usually unbounded: a stray or duplicated release silently raises the permit count above the intended ceiling, and the bound is gone until the process restarts. Use a bounded form (BoundedSemaphore, Semaphore with fairness) to detect this class of bug.

A permit lost on an error, early return, panic or cancellation path shrinks capacity permanently; under sustained traffic the service slowly starves with no error to point at. Always release in a finally/defer/RAII construct.

Blocking acquisition couples the caller's latency to the slowest holder: without a timeout or cancellation the wait is unbounded, so one stuck holder becomes an unbounded queue of stuck waiters. Use try-acquire with a deadline or wrap with wait_for/asyncio.wait_for.

Fairness is a trade: FIFO ordering avoids starvation but costs throughput through hand-off and context switches, while non-fair barging can starve an unlucky waiter indefinitely under high contention.

It bounds concurrency, not rate: a holder may release and reacquire immediately, so a 'N per second' quota is not enforced - conflating the two produces a limit that is simultaneously too loose and too strict. Use a token-bucket rate limiter separately for rate enforcement.

Several semaphores reintroduce deadlock: a task holding one permit and waiting for another can deadlock, so acquisition order or try-with-backoff has to be designed deliberately. When acquiring multiple semaphores, always acquire in consistent order or use try-acquire with exponential backoff.

In-process semaphores bound one process only: each replica gets its own N permits, so a shared downstream quota needs an inter-process or externally coordinated limiter (e.g., a distributed rate limiter, Redis-based token bucket, or a shared proxy).

participants.responsibility: Owns the permit counter and the queue of blocked acquirers: acquire() atomically decrements the counter or blocks, release() increments it and wakes a waiter; the implementation decides fairness (FIFO) or barging. Many implementations (Java Semaphore, Go golang.org/x/sync/semaphore) support context-aware cancellation so blocked acquirers can be interrupted.

The token returned by a successful acquire and returned by release; in RAII languages (C++, Rust, Python with context managers) it is a value whose destruction or drop releases the permit automatically, guaranteeing release on every exit path including panics and cancellations.
The thread, coroutine or worker that must acquire a permit before touching the resource and release it on every exit path - success, error, timeout and cancellation alike.

The thing whose concurrent use is capped: a connection pool, a set of file handles, a memory budget, a downstream API or an accelerator. The resource itself typically knows nothing about the semaphore.

What happens when no permit is available - block, block with a deadline, try and fail fast, or shed load with a distinguishable error; it is part of the pattern's configuration, not an implementation detail. This decision determines whether the semaphore acts as a queue (backpressure) or a rejection gate.

use_cases: Bounding connections to a database or downstream API: acquire a permit before checking out a connection, so a fan-out burst can never drain the client library's pool.
Limiting concurrent file or socket handles in a crawler, indexer or media pipeline where the operating system's descriptor limit is the real ceiling.
Capping parallel work in a batch job (at most N workers at a time) without building a full thread pool when the workers are created elsewhere.
Bounding memory-hungry or CPU-heavy operations - image and PDF transforms, model inference - to the number the machine can actually run concurrently.
Protecting a third-party API with a documented concurrency quota ('at most 5 simultaneous requests') rather than a per-second rate limit.

Serving as the counting gate of a bounded-buffer hand-off: 'empty' and 'full' permits in a producer-consumer protocol, or a one-permit signal released from a different thread or interrupt handler. This is the classic pattern from Dijkstra's EWD 123 and The Little Book of Semaphores.
Serialising a shared test fixture (a database, a port, a temporary directory) with a one-permit semaphore while the rest of the suite stays parallel.

Implementing a token-bucket rate limiter where a background thread or timer refills permits at a steady rate, and callers acquire a permit before each operation, providing controlled bursty throughput without the semaphore acting as a rate limiter itself.

Bounding goroutine parallelism in Go: a buffered channel of capacity N (chan struct{}) serves as an idiomatic semaphore, where sending acquires and receiving releases, providing natural backpressure for I/O-bound workloads.

Weighted resource allocation: an operation requiring k units acquires k permits, enabling fine-grained control over heterogeneous workloads (e.g., large requests taking more connection pool permits) - supported natively by golang.org/x/sync/semaphore.Weighted and Java's acquire(int permits) variant.

Semaphore-based bulkheads in resilience libraries: Resilience4j's SemaphoreBulkhead caps in-flight calls to a dependency at maxConcurrentCalls and waits at most maxWaitDuration before rejecting with BulkheadFullException - a counting semaphore with the admission policy made configurable.

Throttling outbound requests in async Rust: an Arc<tokio::sync::Semaphore> shared across tasks with one permit acquired per request; acquire_many covers weighted work and add_permits adjusts the ceiling at runtime, with release happening automatically when the permit is dropped.

Async-friendly throttling in .NET: SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync awaits a permit without pinning a thread-pool thread, the primitive Microsoft Learn documents for limiting concurrent access to a resource or pool inside a single process.
avoid_when: The concern is requests per second rather than simultaneous users: a token-bucket rate limiter (Rate Limiting) is the right primitive, and a semaphore will not spread work over time.
Only one operation may run at a time and the same thread both takes and returns it: an ordinary mutex or lock is simpler and enforces ownership.

The capacity belongs to one keyed partition (tenant, dependency, route) and each needs its own budget: a bulkhead or per-key limiter expresses that directly, whereas one semaphore gives a single global ceiling.
The resource is a queue of work whose capacity is what matters: a bounded queue or load leveller already blocks producers when full, so a separate counter only duplicates the bound.
The dependency fails hard and fast rather than saturating: a circuit breaker plus a timeout addresses that without a permit counter.
The work is CPU-bound and the pool size is already fixed by an executor or worker pool: the worker count is the semaphore, and a second bound only hides the real one.

Fairness is required and the semaphore implementation does not support it: non-fair semaphores can starve waiters indefinitely under high contention, so a fair semaphore or a separate FIFO queue is needed.
anti_patterns: Using a semaphore as a rate limiter ('100 permits per second'), so bursts still hit the resource all at once and the number is tuned to the wrong unit.
Releasing only on the success path (no finally, defer or RAII), leaking permits until the service starves and the effective ceiling reaches zero.
Unbounded acquisition - acquire() with no timeout or cancellation - so one stuck holder becomes an unbounded queue of blocked callers and the outage spreads.
Releasing without having acquired (or releasing twice), which silently raises the permit count past its ceiling because a semaphore has no owner.
Hard-coding the permit count at each call site, so every caller bounds the same resource differently and the effective limit is the sum of the guesses.
Holding a permit across a long unrelated operation (user interaction, retry loop with sleeps), which converts a resource bound into an accidental lock on capacity.
Acquiring several semaphores in inconsistent order, producing classic deadlock with a resource-exhaustion symptom.
Using asyncio.Semaphore in a threading context or threading.Semaphore inside an async coroutine without an executor, blocking the event loop.
design_principles: Explicit resource budgeting: concurrency limits are declared numbers owned by the component that uses the resource, not emergent properties of thread creation.
Single responsibility at the admission point: the semaphore owns admission, the resource owner owns the resource, and neither needs to know the other's internals.
Fail-safe release: acquire/release must survive exceptions, cancellation and panics (finally, defer, RAII permit, withPermit), because a leaked permit is permanent capacity loss.
Bounded waiting: every wait has a deadline or a cancellation path; unbounded blocking is treated as a bug rather than as a queue.
Measure before sizing: the permit count is derived from the resource's real capacity and validated by load test, then revisited when capacity or traffic shape changes.
Bounded form by default: prefer semaphore implementations that detect over-release, so logic errors fail loudly rather than silently widening the concurrency ceiling.
Composition over configuration: combine semaphores with timeouts, circuit breakers and rate limiters rather than asking the semaphore to be all three.
best_practices: Acquire immediately before using the resource and release in a finally/defer/RAII construct; never let the permit outlive the operation it protects.
Bound the wait: use try-acquire with a deadline (or cancellation-aware acquisition) and decide explicitly whether an unavailable permit means queueing, fast rejection or a degraded fallback.
Size the permit count from measured capacity - the resource's hard limit minus headroom - and keep it configurable instead of copying a number from an example.

Prefer a bounded/max-count form where the language offers one (Python BoundedSemaphore, C# SemaphoreSlim with maxCount, Java Semaphore, Go golang.org/x/sync/semaphore with release-time checks) so over-release fails loudly instead of silently widening the limit.
Keep one semaphore per bounded resource (or per keyed partition) and make it the only admission path to that resource.
Compose with timeouts and circuit breakers: the semaphore bounds how many callers are inside, the timeout bounds how long one may stay, the breaker stops calls that cannot succeed.
Instrument the semaphore - available permits, queue length, wait time - so saturation is visible before users notice it.

In Python, use asyncio.Semaphore for coroutine contexts and threading.Semaphore for thread contexts; never mix them. For cross-context limiting, use a shared lockable primitive designed for the target concurrency model.
In Go, prefer golang.org/x/sync/semaphore.Weighted with context for cancellation-aware weighted acquisition; fall back to a buffered channel (chan struct{}) for simple N-at-a-time limiting.
In Java, use Semaphore(N, fair=true) when starvation is unacceptable; use tryAcquire with timeout to implement shed-load behavior rather than unbounded queuing.
When using multiple semaphores, establish a global acquisition order and apply it consistently; or use try-acquire with exponential backoff to break potential deadlocks automatically.
